lessons.title: The Sun, Light and Shadow
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A shadow is formed on the opposite side of the light, where the light cannot reach because something blocks it.
  • There are four cardinal directions: North, East, South and West.
  • The shadow is long in the morning and evening and short at noon.
  • We can guess the time with the help of the size of a shadow.
  • Writing the names of places around your home and drawing your school are practical activities — every student does them for his or her own home and school.

Activity (book p. 3)

Q: Below is the picture of your home. Write names of places surrounding it.

Ans: Note: This is a personal activity with no single written answer. Every student will write the names of the places around his or her own home. The picture in the book shows the directions North and East to help the student find the direction of each place.

Activity (book p. 4)

Q: i. Shadow is formed on which side of the candle?

Ans: The shadow is formed on the opposite side of the light. The book says a shadow is always formed on the other side, where the light cannot reach because something blocks it. So the shadow of the hand appears on the wall on the opposite side of the candle light.

Q: ii. What happens to the size of the shadow when hand is brought closer to the candle?

Ans: Note: The book does not state what happens to the size of the shadow when the hand is brought closer to the candle. The book only states that the shape and size of a shadow depends on the direction and angle of light. This answer is to be found by doing the classroom observation.

Q: iii. What happens to the shadow when hand is moved away from candle?

Ans: Note: The book does not state what happens to the shadow when the hand is moved away from the candle. The book only states that the shape and size of a shadow depends on the direction and angle of light. This answer is to be found by doing the classroom observation.

Q: iv. When hand is moved to the other side of the candle, shadow is formed on which side?

Ans: The shadow is formed on the opposite side of the light. When the hand is moved to the other side of the candle, the shadow also changes side and appears on the side opposite to the hand and the candle light.

Practical Work (book p. 6)

Q: i. Draw a sketch of your school and point out important places situated at North, South, East and West of it.

Ans: Note: This is a practical drawing activity with no written answer. Every student will draw his or her own school and write the names of the important places in the North, South, East and West of it.

Q: ii. Stand in the lawn of your home and school according to the schedule given in the table (8 am, 12 noon, 4 pm). Observe the shadows of yourself and other things and complete the table (Size of Shadow, Direction of shadow).

Ans: Note: This is a practical observation activity with no fixed written answer. The student observes and writes the size and direction of the shadow at 8 am, 12 noon and 4 pm. The book states that the shadow is long at morning and evening and short at noon time, and that we can guess time with the help of shadow.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The Earth revolves around the Sun in its orbit.
  • The Sun sets in the West and seems to rise in the East.
  • Light travels in a straight line; when something blocks it, a shadow is formed on the other side.
  • The size of a shadow changes at different times of the day.

Exercise — 1. Fill in the blanks with suitable words (book p. 5)

Q: i. The Earth revolves around the _____ in its orbit.

Ans: Sun

Q: ii. We can guess _____ with the help of size of a shadow.

Ans: time

Q: iii. Shadow is formed on the _____ side of light.

Ans: opposite

Q: iv. Sun sets in the _____.

Ans: West

Q: v. Shadow is _____ at morning and evening.

Ans: long

Exercise — 2. With the help of the following pictures, point out morning, noon and evening (book p. 5)

Q: With the help of the pictures of the Sun and the tree, point out morning, noon and evening.

Ans: In the picture where the Sun is low in the East and the shadow of the tree is long, it is morning. In the picture where the Sun is high above the tree and the shadow is short, it is noon. In the picture where the Sun is low in the West and the shadow is long, it is evening. The book says the shadow is long at morning and evening and short at noon time.

Exercise — 3. Read the following statements carefully and mark them with correct or wrong (book p. 5)

Q: True or False: i. East is opposite to North.

Ans: False

Q: True or False: ii. Size of a shadow varies at different times of the day.

Ans: True

Q: True or False: iii. Shadows are longer than their real size at morning and evening.

Ans: True

Q: True or False: iv. Time can be guessed with the help of changes in the shadow.

Ans: True

Q: True or False: v. Light travels in straight line.

Ans: True

Exercise — Q4. Answer the following questions (book p. 6)

Q: i. Write cardinal directions.

Ans: There are four cardinal directions. They are North, East, West and South. Directions help us to know the position of a place or a thing.

Q: ii. How is shadow formed?

Ans: Rays of light travel in straight lines from their source. If something blocks the light on its way, the light cannot pass through it. Then the shadow of that thing is formed on the other side. Light is necessary for the formation of a shadow.

Q: iii. Why Sun seems rising in the East?

Ans: Actually the Sun does not rise and set. The Earth revolves around the Sun in its orbit from West to East. Due to this revolution, the Sun seems rising in the East and setting in the West.

mcqs.q: The Earth revolves around the _____ in its orbit.
mcqs.why: The Earth revolves around the Sun in its orbit. The Sun is at the centre and the Earth goes around it.

mcqs.q: We can guess _____ with the help of the size of a shadow.
mcqs.why: The book says we can guess time with the help of the size of a shadow, because the size of the shadow changes during the day.

mcqs.q: A shadow is formed on the _____ side of the light.
mcqs.why: A shadow is always formed on the opposite side of the light, where the light cannot reach because something blocks it.

mcqs.q: The Sun sets in the _____.
mcqs.why: The Sun seems to rise in the East and sets in the West. West is the direction opposite to East.

mcqs.q: The shadow is _____ in the morning and evening.
mcqs.why: The book says the shadow is long at morning and evening and short at noon time, when the Sun is high above.

mcqs.q: How many cardinal directions are there?
mcqs.why: There are four cardinal directions: North, East, West and South. Directions help us to know the position of a place or a thing.

mcqs.q: East is opposite to _____.
mcqs.why: East is opposite to West, not to North. North is opposite to South, so the statement 'East is opposite to North' is wrong.

mcqs.q: How is a shadow formed?
mcqs.why: Rays of light travel in straight lines. If something blocks the light on its way, the light cannot pass through it, and the shadow of that thing is formed on the other side.

mcqs.q: In the picture where the Sun is high above the tree and the shadow is short, it is _____.
mcqs.why: At noon the Sun is high above the tree and the shadow is short. In the morning and evening the Sun is low and the shadow is long.

mcqs.q: Light travels in a _____ line.
mcqs.why: The book says light travels in a straight line from its source. That is why a thing that blocks the light makes a shadow on the other side.

lessons.title: Goods, Services and Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Natural resources include water, land, air, forests, minerals, rivers and ocean.
  • Human resources include farmers, carpenters, police and doctors.
  • Capital resources include dams, vehicles, factories and machines.
  • Goods are material things, for example a computer, chair, tractor, pencil and chocolate.
  • Services are the ways people serve one another, for example teaching, driving and repairing a bicycle.

Activity (book p. 9)

Q: Collect pictures of natural, human and capital resources. Make an album of these pictures.

Ans: Note: This is a practical cut-and-paste activity with no written answer. The student collects pictures and makes an album. From the book: natural resources include water, land, air, forests, minerals, rivers and ocean; human resources include farmers, carpenters, police and doctors; capital resources include dams, vehicles, factories and machines.

Activity — Separate goods and services (book p. 9)

Q: Below is a list of goods and services. Separate them and write them in their respective column. Repairing Bicycle, Polishing Shoes, Computer, Chair, Teaching, Tractor, Examination of Teeth, Driving, Pencil, chocolate.

Ans: Goods: Computer, Chair, Tractor, Pencil, chocolate. Services: Repairing Bicycle, Polishing Shoes, Teaching, Examination of Teeth, Driving. Goods are material things, while services are the ways people serve one another.

Activity (book p. 10)

Q: Prepare a list of five goods and five services of your area.

Ans: Note: This is a personal activity with no single written answer. Every student will list the goods and services found in his or her own area. The book gives examples of goods such as bread, fruits and shoes, and examples of services such as doctor, teacher, tailor and carpenter.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a good?
mcqs.why: Goods are material things. A chair is a material thing, while teaching, driving and polishing shoes are services — ways people serve one another.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a service?
mcqs.why: Services are the ways people serve one another. Repairing a bicycle is work done for others; a computer, tractor and pencil are goods.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a natural resource?
mcqs.why: Rivers are given by nature, so a river is a natural resource. Factories, bicycles and aeroplanes are made by human beings.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a human resource?
mcqs.why: Human resources are people who work with their skill and ability, like a dentist. Forests, mountains and natural gas are natural resources.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a capital resource?
mcqs.why: Capital resources are made by human beings, for example dams, vehicles, factories and machines. Water, land and air are natural resources given by nature.

mcqs.q: Teaching is an example of a _____.
mcqs.why: Services are the ways people serve one another in daily life. Teaching is a service, like the work of a doctor, teacher, tailor and carpenter.

mcqs.q: Chocolate is a _____.
mcqs.why: In the book's activity, chocolate is placed with the goods: computer, chair, tractor, pencil and chocolate. Goods are material things we need in daily life.

mcqs.q: Examination of teeth is a _____.
mcqs.why: Examination of teeth is the work a dentist does for others, so it is a service. Services are the ways people serve one another.

mcqs.q: Which group contains only natural resources?
mcqs.why: Natural resources are given by nature: water, land, air, forests, minerals, rivers and ocean. The other groups are capital resources, human resources and goods.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a human resource?
mcqs.why: Human resources include farmers, carpenters, police and doctors. A dam and a machine are capital resources, and a forest is a natural resource.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • There are three kinds of resources: natural, human and capital resources.
  • When goods and services are less than required, the situation is called scarcity.
  • Buying a substitute when we cannot buy the thing we desire is called economic choice.
  • We need other people in our daily life; this is called interdependence.
  • A person who buys goods is a buyer and a person who sells goods is a seller.

Exercise — Q1. Write the given resources in their relevant columns (book p. 12)

Q: Write the given resources in their relevant columns: rivers, forests, aeroplane, tailor, dentist, natural gas, driver, bicycle, scientist, lawyer, desert, factory, power house, mountains, tube well.

Ans: Natural Resources: rivers, forests, natural gas, desert, mountains. Human Resources: tailor, dentist, driver, scientist, lawyer. Capital Resources: aeroplane, bicycle, factory, power house, tube well.

Exercise — Q2. Answer the following questions (book p. 12)

Q: i. I bought a story book. What am I? (Buyer)

Ans: You are a buyer. People who buy goods and services made by other people are called buyers.

Q: ii. I wanted to buy a large ice cream for Rs. 100, but I had only Rs. 60. So, I bought a smaller one for Rs. 60. What is this decision called?

Ans: This decision is called economic choice. When people cannot buy the thing they desire due to lack of resources, scarcity and increasing prices, they buy a substitute of that thing. This is called economic choice.

Q: iii. Sugar is not available in the market. What is this situation called?

Ans: This situation is called scarcity. When goods, resources and services are less than required, people face problems. This situation is called scarcity.

Q: iv. We need other people in our daily life. What is this called?

Ans: This is called interdependence. We cannot do all the jobs ourselves nor make everything we need. Therefore we need other persons. This is called interdependence.

Q: v. What is a person called who sells goods?

Ans: A person who sells goods and services is called a seller.

Exercise — Q3. Match column (A) with (B) (book p. 13)

Q: Match: Shortage of goods and services

Ans: Scarcity

Q: Match: Products of natural and material resources

Ans: Goods

Q: Match: Human skill, ability and specialization

Ans: Human resources

Q: Match: Treatment of patients

Ans: Services

Q: Match: Use of substitutes due to scarcity or dearness

Ans: Economic choice

Exercise — Q4. Answer briefly (book p. 13)

Q: i. How many resources are there? Give example of each.

Ans: There are three kinds of resources. Natural resources, for example water, land, air and forests. Human resources, for example farmers, carpenters, police and doctors. Capital resources, for example dams, vehicles, factories and machines.

Q: ii. What is scarcity?

Ans: When goods, resources and services are less than required, people face problems. This situation is called scarcity. For example, sometimes there is scarcity of petrol, sugar and flour.

Q: iii. Why do we depend on others in our daily life?

Ans: We depend on others because we cannot do all the jobs ourselves nor make everything we need. We need many goods and services to live, and we cannot make everything ourselves, so we buy goods and services made by other people.

Q: iv. What is the difference between goods and services?

Ans: Goods are the material things we need in our daily life, for example bread, fruits and shoes. They are the products of natural and man-made resources. Services are the ways people serve one another in their daily life, for example doctor, teacher, tailor and carpenter.

Q: v. Why do we opt for substitutes?

Ans: We opt for substitutes because people do not have enough resources. They fail to buy the things they desire due to lack of resources, scarcity and increasing prices of things. Therefore they buy substitutes of those things.

Q: vi. Can we lead a good life without interdependence?

Ans: No, we cannot lead a good life without interdependence. We cannot do all the jobs ourselves nor make everything we need. Therefore we need other persons in our daily life.

mcqs.why: Rivers, forests, natural gas, desert and mountains are natural resources because they are given by nature.

mcqs.why: People who work with skill and ability are human resources. The book places tailor, dentist, driver, scientist and lawyer in human resources.

mcqs.why: Capital resources are made by human beings, for example aeroplane, bicycle, factory, power house and tube well.

mcqs.why: When people cannot buy the thing they desire due to lack of resources, scarcity and increasing prices, they buy a substitute of that thing. This decision is called economic choice.

mcqs.q: We need other people in our daily life. This is called _____.
mcqs.why: We cannot do all the jobs ourselves nor make everything we need. Therefore we need other persons in our daily life. This is called interdependence.

mcqs.q: A person who sells goods and services is called a _____.
mcqs.why: The book says a person who sells goods and services is called a seller, and a person who buys them is called a buyer.

mcqs.q: How many kinds of resources are there?
mcqs.why: There are three kinds of resources: natural resources, human resources and capital resources.

mcqs.q: Treatment of patients is an example of _____.
mcqs.why: In the matching exercise of the book, treatment of patients matches with services, because services are the ways people serve one another.

lessons.title: Saving Our Natural Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Water, electricity and gas shall be used according to the needs; rain water shall be stored.
  • Nature has offered natural resources in limited quantity, so they must be used carefully.
  • Endangered animals named in the book are the Indus dolphin, snow leopard, black deer, markhor, brown bear and marcopolo sheep.
  • Making charts and collecting pictures are practical activities done by the students themselves.

Activity (book p. 15)

Q: Make a chart. Illustrate how can you conserve water, gas and electricity at home.

Ans: Note: This is a practical chart-making activity with no single written answer. The book states that water, electricity and gas shall be used according to the needs, rain water shall be stored, and water drained from factories and houses shall be cleaned for usage.

Activity (book p. 17)

Q: Observe your surrounding and tell that the following resources are used for which purpose: Land, Water, Crude oil.

Ans: Note: This is an observation and oral activity based on the student's own surroundings, so it has no single written answer in the book. The book does not state the purposes of land, water and crude oil for this table. The book only states that air, water, forests and minerals are natural resources and nature has offered these in limited quantity.

Activity (book p. 18)

Q: Collect pictures of endangered animals from different sources. Get information about them and arrange an exhibition in the classroom.

Ans: Note: This is a practical activity with no written answer. The student collects pictures and arranges a classroom exhibition. The book names these endangered animals: Indus dolphin, snow leopard, black deer, markhor, brown bear and marcopolo sheep.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Endangered animals in the book are markhor, brown bear, marcopolo sheep and black deer.
  • Extinct animals are those which once lived but are no longer found on Earth, for example dinosaur, dodo bird and Tasmanian tiger.
  • If forests are cut, animals and birds will be unable to live and the temperature will rise.
  • To protect endangered animals, hunting should be banned and more trees should be planted.

Exercise — Q1. Identify endangered and extinct animals in the pictures given below (book p. 20)

Q: Identify endangered and extinct animals in the pictures given below. Circle the endangered animals in red and extinct animals in blue colours. Pictures: Jelly fish, Dodo Bird, Markhor, Cow, Rabbit, Tasmanian tiger, Brown Bear, Lion, Dinosaur, Marcopolo Sheep, Crow, Black Deer.

Ans: Endangered animals (circle in red): Markhor, Brown Bear, Marcopolo Sheep, Black Deer. Extinct animals (circle in blue): Dodo Bird, Tasmanian tiger, Dinosaur. The other animals in the pictures — Jelly fish, Cow, Rabbit, Lion and Crow — are neither endangered nor extinct in this book.

Exercise — Q2. What would happen if (book p. 20)

Q: i. What would happen if natural gas is exhausted?

Ans: Natural gas is a mineral found in the land. The book says scarcity of minerals available in land like coal, oil and gas will cause shortage of energy. It will create a lot of problems for human beings.

Q: ii. What would happen if minerals are exhausted?

Ans: If minerals are exhausted, there will be a shortage of energy. The book says scarcity of minerals available in land like coal, oil and gas will cause shortage of energy and it will create a lot of problems for human beings.

Q: iii. What would happen if deforestation occurs?

Ans: Forests are the habitat of animals. Due to lack of forests, animals and birds will be unable to live and the temperature will also rise.

Exercise — Q3. Suggest two methods for preservation of each resource (book p. 21)

Q: Suggest two methods for the preservation of Water.

Ans: i. Water shall be used according to the needs. ii. Rain water shall be stored. The book also says water drained from factories and houses shall be cleaned for usage.

Q: Suggest two methods for the preservation of Forest.

Ans: i. Trees shall not be cut needlessly. ii. New plants and trees shall be planted to replace the cut trees.

Q: Suggest two methods for the preservation of Air.

Ans: Note: The book does not give separate methods for the preservation of air. It gives general measures for the conservation of natural resources, which include: i. Alternate sources of energy like solar and wind energy shall be used. ii. Garbage shall be used to produce energy.

Exercise — Q4. Write short answers to the following questions (book p. 21)

Q: i. Name any three human activities which are harmful for natural environment.

Ans: Three human activities harmful for the natural environment are: i. Deforestation for fulfilling the needs of the growing population. ii. Smoke of factories and vehicles. iii. Garbage of houses, factories and hospitals. The book also lists polluted water from homes and factories, use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, and noise produced by aeroplane, vehicles and machines.

Q: ii. What kind of problems will water scarcity create?

Ans: Scarcity of water will make the land barren. Crops will not be grown, which will cause starvation.

Q: iii. What should be done to protect endangered animals?

Ans: To protect endangered animals: i. Forestation should be done, because forests are the habitat of animals. ii. Hunting of endangered animals should be banned. iii. Awareness about endangered animals should be increased among the people.

Q: iv. Describe any three steps for preventing natural resources from destruction.

Ans: Three steps are: i. Natural resources shall be used carefully according to the need. ii. Trees shall not be cut needlessly. iii. New plants and trees shall be planted to replace the cut trees.

Q: v. What is meant by extinct animals?

Ans: Those animals which once lived but today no animal of their species is found on Earth are called extinct animals. For example, Dinosaur, Dodo bird, Tasmanian tiger and Wild bull.

lessons.title: About Quaid-e-Azam
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The real name of Quaid-e-Azam was Muhammad Ali Jinnah.
  • He was born on 25 December 1876 in Karachi.
  • He got higher studies in law in England and then practised law in India.
  • He is called the founder of Pakistan and the father of the nation.
  • He died on 11 September 1948 and his tomb is in Karachi.

Activity (book p. 23)

Q: Get more information about Quaid-e-Azam from your grandparents. Hang these information in classroom in the form of a chart.

Ans: Note: This is a practical classroom activity. There is no written answer in the book. Students ask their grandparents about Quaid-e-Azam and display the collected information on a chart in the classroom.

Q2. Give the following information about Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. (book p. 25)

Q: Name:

Ans: Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The book says the real name of Quaid-e-Azam was Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

Q: Date of birth:

Ans: December 25, 1876.

Q: Place of birth:

Ans: Karachi.

Q: Profession:

Ans: Law. He got higher studies in law in England and, on his return to India, he started practicing law.

Q: The most important achievement:

Ans: He united the Muslims of India and demanded a separate country for them. Pakistan came into being on August 14, 1947, so he is called the founder of Pakistan.

Q: Titles:

Ans: Quaid-e-Azam, founder of Pakistan and father of the nation.

Q: Date of death:

Ans: September 11, 1948.

Q: Tomb:

Ans: Karachi. His tomb is in Karachi.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Quaid-e-Azam was the first Governor General of Pakistan.
  • He started his political life in 1906.
  • He demanded a separate country for Muslims in the Lahore Resolution in 1940.
  • His three guiding principles are Faith, Unity and Discipline.
  • His greatest quality was his punctuality; he was also truthful, honest and hardworking.

Q1. Choose the correct option. (book p. 24)

Q: i. Quaid-e-Azam was born on 25th _____, 1876. (a) September (b) November (c) December

Ans: December

Q: ii. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah received his higher education from _____. (a) Germany (b) India (c) England

Ans: England

Q: iii. Quaid-e-Azam was the first _____ of Pakistan. (a) president (b) prime minister (c) governor general

Ans: governor general

Q: iv. In _____ Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah started his political life. (a) 1906 (b) 1913 (c) 1916

Ans: 1906

Q: v. The tomb of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah is in _____. (a) Quetta (b) Peshawar (c) Karachi

Ans: Karachi

Q3. Give short answers. (book p. 25)

Q: i. Why Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah is called the founder of Pakistan?

Ans: He is called the founder of Pakistan because he united the Muslims of India, demanded a separate country for Muslims in the Lahore Resolution in 1940, and Pakistan came into being on August 14, 1947. The book also calls him father of the nation because of this achievement.

Q: ii. Why did Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah make a separate country?

Ans: He realised that the rights of Muslims in India would not be protected after getting independence from the British. Therefore, he demanded a separate country for Muslims so that their rights could be protected.

Q: iii. Describe the three guiding principles of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

Ans: The three guiding principles given by Quaid-e-Azam are Faith, Unity and Discipline. The book says we can make Pakistan a great and developed country by acting upon these principles.

Q: iv. Describe any four qualities of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

Ans: Four qualities given in the book are: he was truthful, he was honest, he was hardworking, and he had love for justice. The book also says his greatest quality was his punctuality.

lessons.title: How Living Things Change
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Some offsprings are like their parents at the time of birth, for example lion, cat, dog and human beings.
  • Some offsprings are not like their parents at birth, for example butterfly, frog and mosquito.
  • The larva is the second stage of the life cycle of an insect and the pupa is the third stage.
  • A tadpole is the second stage of the life cycle of a frog.
  • The life cycle of a plant has four stages, from seed to flower and new seeds.

Look at the pictures (book p. 30)

Q: Look at the pictures carefully. What changes do you observe?

Ans: The pictures show living things changing as they grow. The caterpillar changes and becomes a butterfly, and the small puppy grows into a big dog. The book says some offsprings are like their parents at the time of birth, while some are not like their parents at birth and later assume the form of their parents.

Activity (book p. 30)

Q: Below are the names of different animals. Draw a circle around those similar to their parents at the time of birth. cat, butterfly, lion, frog, mosquito, human beings.

Ans: Circle: cat, lion and human beings. The book says offsprings of lion, goat and dog are like their parents in form and shape at the time of birth, and its Key Points also give cat in this group. Butterfly and frog are given in the book as not like their parents at the time of birth, and a mosquito is an insect born from eggs, so it is also not circled.

Activity (book p. 31)

Q: Draw the stages of life cycle of sunflower.

Ans: Note: This is a drawing activity with no written answer. The book gives the life cycle of plants in four stages, for example the bean plant: 1st stage seed is sown in the soil, 2nd stage plant comes out of the seed, 3rd stage plant grows in size, 4th stage flowers are grown on plants and seeds are formed in flowers. Draw the sunflower in these same four stages.

Activity (book p. 32)

Q: What is the difference between i. Larva and butterfly?

Ans: Larva is the second stage of the life cycle of an insect, when eggs develop into larva. A butterfly is the grown insect of the last stage, when the pupa develops into an insect.

Q: What is the difference between ii. Tadpole and frog?

Ans: A tadpole is the second stage of the life cycle of a frog, when eggs develop into tadpoles. A frog is the grown animal of the third stage, when tadpoles completely grow into frogs.

Q: What is the difference between iii. Larva and pupa?

Ans: Larva is the second stage of the life cycle of an insect and pupa is the third stage. In the third stage, the larva develops into the pupa, and then the pupa develops into an insect.

mcqs.q: Which animal is like its parents at the time of birth?
mcqs.why: Offsprings of lion, goat, dog and cat are like their parents in form and shape at the time of birth. Butterfly, frog and mosquito are not like their parents at birth.

mcqs.q: Which animal is NOT like its parents at the time of birth?
mcqs.why: A frog is born as a tadpole and later assumes the form of its parents, so it is not like its parents at birth. Lion, dog and human beings are like their parents at birth.

mcqs.q: Larva is the _____ stage of the life cycle of an insect.
mcqs.why: In the life cycle of an insect, eggs develop into larva in the second stage. The pupa is the third stage and the grown insect is the last stage.

mcqs.q: Pupa is the _____ stage of the life cycle of an insect.
mcqs.why: Larva is the second stage and pupa is the third stage. In the third stage, the larva develops into the pupa, and then the pupa develops into an insect.

mcqs.q: A tadpole is the _____ stage of the life cycle of a frog.
mcqs.why: A tadpole is the second stage of the life cycle of a frog, when eggs develop into tadpoles. A frog is the grown animal of the third stage.

mcqs.q: In the last stage of the life cycle of an insect, the pupa develops into _____.
mcqs.why: A butterfly is the grown insect of the last stage, when the pupa develops into an insect.

mcqs.q: The caterpillar changes and becomes a _____.
mcqs.why: The pictures in the book show living things changing as they grow: the caterpillar changes and becomes a butterfly, and the small puppy grows into a big dog.

mcqs.q: In the first stage of the life cycle of a plant, _____.
options: the seed is sown in the soil
mcqs.why: The life cycle of a plant has four stages: in the 1st stage the seed is sown in the soil, in the 2nd stage the plant comes out of the seed, in the 3rd stage the plant grows in size, and in the 4th stage flowers grow and seeds are formed.

mcqs.q: In the fourth stage of the life cycle of a plant, _____.
options: flowers are grown and seeds are formed in flowers
the seed is sown in the soil
the plant comes out of the seed
mcqs.why: The last stage is the fourth stage. In this stage, flowers are grown on plants and seeds are formed in flowers.

mcqs.q: Which of these animals are similar to their parents at the time of birth?
mcqs.why: The book's activity circles cat, lion and human beings. Butterfly and frog are not like their parents at the time of birth, and a mosquito is an insect born from eggs.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The period of plants and animals from birth to reproduction is called life cycle.
  • The life cycle of birds has three stages: eggs, chicks and grown birds.
  • The life cycle of insects has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and insect.
  • In the last stage of the life cycle of plants, flowers grow and seeds are formed in the flowers.

Q1. Complete the following table. (book p. 33)

Q: Complete the table: Organisms which are similar to their parents at the time of birth (i, ii, iii) and Organisms which are different from their parents at the time of birth (i, ii, iii).

Ans: Similar to their parents at the time of birth: i. lion, ii. cat, iii. dog. Different from their parents at the time of birth: i. butterfly, ii. frog, iii. mosquito. The book gives lion, goat and dog as examples of the first group and frog and butterfly as examples of the second group.

Q2. Fill in the blanks (book p. 34)

Q: The life cycle of butterfly is shown in the pictures. Top left picture (an adult butterfly with wings): _____

Ans: Butterfly

Q: The life cycle of butterfly is shown in the pictures. Top right picture (eggs on a leaf): _____

Ans: Egg

Ans: Pupa

Q: The life cycle of butterfly is shown in the pictures. Bottom right picture (a caterpillar on a leaf): _____

Ans: Larva

Q3. Write short answers of the following questions. (book p. 34)

Q: i. What is meant by life cycle?

Ans: The period of plants and animals from birth to reproduction is called life cycle. Living organisms pass through different stages after their birth and growth, and the life cycle of plants and animals consists of different stages.

Q: ii. Are the life cycle of plants and animals are similar?

Ans: No. The life cycle of plants and animals consists of different stages. For example, the life cycle of plants consists of four stages, the life cycle of birds has three stages and the life cycle of insects consists of four stages.

Q: iii. Write stages of life cycle of birds.

Ans: The life cycle of birds consists of three stages. In the first stage, birds lay eggs. In the second stage, chicks come out of eggs. In the third stage, chicks grow into birds. The book gives the life cycle of a hen as an example.

Q: iv. What happens in the last stage of life cycle of plants?

Ans: The last stage is the fourth stage. In this stage, flowers are grown on plants and seeds are formed in flowers.

mcqs.why: The green case hanging from a twig is the pupa stage. The caterpillar on a leaf is the larva and the adult with wings is the butterfly.

lessons.title: Habitats of Living Things
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Habitat has two main types: land habitat and water habitat.
  • Land habitats are forest, desert and grassland.
  • Water habitats are fresh water, salty water, coastal habitat and polar regions.
  • Desert animals in the book are camel and ostrich; the desert plant is the cactus.
  • Polar region animals are polar bear, penguin and wolf; fresh water animals are frog and fish.

Activity (book p. 36)

Q: Is light necessary for growth of plants? Take three plants of the same kind. Place one plant in sunlight, the other in dark place and cover the third one in polythene (or in plastic) bag. Give equal amount of water to these three plants on daily basis. Observe the changes occurring in them and write them in the observation table in your note book.

Ans: Note: This is a practical observation activity with no written answer given in the book. You do the experiment and write the height of the plants, the colour of leaves and other changes on the 2nd, 4th and 6th day in the table yourself. The book only states the fact behind it: heat and light are necessary for the maintenance of life, plants prepare their food by using solar energy, and life is not possible without sun.

Activity (book p. 41)

Q: Attach a picture of a bird or animal or plant that can be found in the following habitats: Desert, Forest, Grassland, Polar Region, Fresh Water, Salty Water.

Ans: Note: This is a cut-and-paste picture activity with no written answer in the book. Pictures can be chosen from the examples the book itself gives: Desert - plant: cactus, animal: camel or ostrich; Forest - plant: pine trees or gum arabic trees, animal: lion, wolf, monkey or giraffe; Grassland - plant: grass and bushes, animal: deer, elephant or zebra; Polar Region - plant: plants are present in very little number (no plant is named in the book), animal: polar bear, penguin or wolf; Fresh Water - plant: lilies, animal: frog or fish; Salty Water - plant: sea weed or algae, animal: jelly fish, crab, star fish or sea turtle.

Think! (book p. 42)

Q: Think! How humans adapt themselves to their environment.

Ans: Note: This is a thinking/discussion question. The book does not state how humans adapt themselves to their environment, so no written answer is given in the book. The book only defines adaptation: the appearance of a characteristic in a living organism in a specific habitat due to changing conditions is adaptation, and these adaptations are necessary for getting food, protection from climatic changes and enemies.

Activity - Complete the chart (book p. 45)

Q: Complete the chart: Habitat is divided into Water and Land. Complete the boxes under Water (one box is already filled: Salty Water) and under Land (one box is already filled: Desert).

Ans: Habitat has two main types: Land habitat and Water habitat. Land habitat: Forest, Desert and Grassland. Water habitat: Fresh Water, Salty Water, Coastal Habitat and Polar Regions.

Project Work (book p. 51)

Q: Divide the students in three groups. Give the topic of desert habitat to one group, grassland habitat to second group and fresh water habitat to third group. Every group shall present the obtained information about the given topic in form of chart or model in class.

Ans: Note: This is a group project and class presentation activity with no written answer in the book. The book states: Desert is mostly sandy, hot and dry, it rains very little and there is scarcity of water, for example camel, ostrich and cactus live there; Grassland is a wide area covered by grass and bushes with less trees, and deer, elephant and zebra live there; Fresh water includes rivers, lakes, ponds and streams, and it is the habitat of frogs, fishes and lilies.

mcqs.q: Habitat is divided into two main types: _____.
mcqs.why: Habitat has two main types: Land habitat and Water habitat. Land habitat includes forest, desert and grassland.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a land habitat?
mcqs.why: Land habitats are forest, desert and grassland. Fresh water, salty water and coastal habitat are water habitats.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a water habitat?
mcqs.why: Water habitats are fresh water, salty water, coastal habitat and polar regions. Forest, desert and grassland are land habitats.

mcqs.q: Which plant is found in the desert?
mcqs.why: The book gives cactus as the desert plant and camel or ostrich as desert animals. Lilies grow in fresh water, sea weed in salty water and pine trees in forests.

mcqs.q: Which animal lives in the polar region?
mcqs.why: Polar bear, penguin and wolf are the animals of the polar region in the book. Camel lives in the desert, zebra in grassland and frog in fresh water.

mcqs.q: Frog and fish live in _____.
mcqs.why: Fresh water includes rivers, lakes, ponds and streams, and it is the habitat of frogs, fishes and lilies.

mcqs.q: Jelly fish, crab and star fish live in _____.
mcqs.why: The book gives jelly fish, crab, star fish and sea turtle as animals of salty water, and sea weed or algae as its plants.

mcqs.why: Grassland is a wide area covered by grass and bushes, with less number of trees. Deer, elephant and zebra are the animals of grassland in the book.

mcqs.q: Lion, wolf, monkey and giraffe are animals of the _____.
mcqs.why: The book gives pine trees or gum arabic trees as forest plants and lion, wolf, monkey or giraffe as forest animals.

mcqs.why: Coastal habitat is the area where land and oceans meet; for example, mangrove, swamp grasses and crabs are found here.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The place where organisms live is called their habitat.
  • The Sun is the biggest source of heat and light; plants prepare their food by using sunlight.
  • The ocean is the biggest water habitat and sea water is salty in taste.
  • A camel stores fat in its hump and its soft, wide feet help it to walk on sand.
  • The leaves of water plants are big and flat and their stems are thin and elastic.

Q: i. The _____ is the biggest source of heat and light.

Ans: Sun

Q: ii. For the preparation of _____ plants use sunlight.

Q: Match Column A with Column B: Polar region

Ans: Cold regions

Q: Match Column A with Column B: Grass land

Q4. Write short answers of the following questions. (book p. 49)

Q: i. Define habitat.

Ans: The place where organisms live is called their habitat. Habitat is a natural environment where organisms live, grow and fulfill their needs, which are necessary for life.

Q: ii. Writ three effects of human activities on natural habitats.

Ans: 1. Humans are destroying forests and grassland for constructing buildings, timber and fuel, so plants and animals are deprived from natural habitats and their life is in danger. 2. Water released from factories and homes is polluting water habitats, due to which the lives of living organisms are in serious danger, and the oil released by ships is destroying ocean life. 3. Due to the use of fertilizers and insecticides not only plants and animals are affected but human beings are also effected. As a result, living organisms face scarcity of food, water and space.

Q: iii. Why sun is important for living organisms?

Ans: In universe Earth is the only planet where life exists. Heat and light are necessary for the maintenance of life and its biggest source is sun. This light and heat are called solar energy. Plants prepare their food by using solar energy and other living organisms depend on plants. Life is not possible without sun.

Q: iv. How camel is adapted to desert habitat?

Ans: Camel is an animal of desert. It protects itself from sand by closing its nostrils. The long eyebrows of camel protect eyes from sand particles. Camel stores fats in hump and can live for many days without eating food. The soft and wide feet of camel help it to walk on sand.

Q: v. Write the characteristics of aquatic plants.

Ans: The leaves of the plants which grow in water are big and flat. They help them in swimming in water. Their stems are thin, elastic and submerged in water. For example, lilies.

Q5. Write the types of habitat under the given pictures. (book p. 50)

Q: Picture 1 (top left, tall trees): Write the type of habitat under the picture.

Ans: Forest habitat. Forest is a large area which is covered by green plants and trees.

Q: Picture 2 (top right, wide grassy area with few trees): Write the type of habitat under the picture.

Ans: Grassland habitat. Wide area which is covered by grass and bushes is called grassland.

Q: Picture 3 (middle left, a diver under the sea): Write the type of habitat under the picture.

Ans: Marine (salty water) habitat. Oceans are the biggest water habitats.

Q: Picture 4 (middle right, polar bears on snow): Write the type of habitat under the picture.

Ans: Polar region habitat. Polar regions are the coldest regions and are covered with snow throughout the year.

Q: Picture 5 (bottom left, water with lilies): Write the type of habitat under the picture.

Ans: Fresh water habitat. Rivers, lakes, ponds and streams are included in fresh water, and fresh water is the habitat of frogs, fishes and lilies.

Q: Picture 6 (bottom right, sand dunes): Write the type of habitat under the picture.

Ans: Desert habitat. Deserts are mostly sandy, hot and dry areas.

Q: Picture 7 (bottom centre, trees standing in water at the edge of land and water): Write the type of habitat under the picture.

Ans: Coastal habitat. This is the area where land and oceans meet, for example mangrove, swamp grasses and crabs are found here.

Q6. I am an ostrich, can you tell me how my given characteristics help me in adaptation to desert habitat. (book p. 51)

Ans: Note: The book does not state how the ostrich's long and strong legs help it in the desert. The book only names ostrich as an example of an animal that can live in the desert. No answer for this characteristic is given in the book.

Ans: Note: The book does not state how the ostrich's long and thick eyebrows help it in the desert. For the camel, the book states that long eyebrows protect eyes from sand particles, but it gives no such statement for the ostrich.

Ans: Note: The book does not state how the ostrich's big eyes help it in the desert. No answer for this characteristic is given in the book.

Ans: Note: The book does not state how the ostrich's long elastic neck helps it in the desert. No answer for this characteristic is given in the book.

lessons.title: Food Groups and Balanced Diet
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Animals are divided into three groups on the basis of food: herbivores, carnivores and omnivores.
  • Herbivores eat grass, plants and their fruit, for example rabbit, cow and grasshopper.
  • Carnivores eat the meat of other animals, for example cheetah, lion and polar bear.
  • Omnivores eat meat, plants and their fruits, for example rat and human beings.
  • If we do not eat a balanced diet, the needs of our body are not fulfilled and we do not remain healthy.

Think! (book p. 53)

Q: Do all animals eat the same type of food?

Ans: No. All living organisms do not eat the same type of food. Different animals eat different food. Some animals only eat green plants, some eat meat, and some animals eat both green plants and meat.

Q: Think! Which group do you belong to on the basis of food?

Ans: We belong to the omnivores group. Omnivores eat meat, plants and their fruits, and we also eat both meat and plants and fruits.

Activity (book p. 54)

Q: Write the group of each animal on the basis of food: rabbit, cheetah, grasshopper, rat, polar bear, cow, lion and tortoise (turtle).

Ans: Rabbit — Herbivore (the book gives rabbit as a herbivore; herbivores eat grass, plants and their fruit). Cheetah — Carnivore (the book gives cheetah as a carnivore; carnivores eat the meat of other animals). Grasshopper — Herbivore (it eats plants). Rat — Omnivore (the book gives rat as an omnivore; omnivores eat meat, plants and their fruits). Polar bear — Carnivore (it eats the meat of other animals). Cow — Herbivore (the book gives cow as a herbivore). Lion — Carnivore (the book gives lion as a carnivore). Tortoise — Herbivore (it eats plants and leaves).

Think! and Activity (book p. 57)

Q: Think! What will be the result, if we do not eat balanced diet?

Ans: If we do not use a balanced diet, then the needs of our body are not fulfilled and we do not remain healthy.

Q: Activity: Write names of two vegetables and fruits which you like and complete the table (Name: Vegetable/Fruit, Season in which found, Colour).

Ans: Note: This is a personal-choice writing activity. There is no single fixed written answer in the book, because every student will write the vegetables and fruits he or she likes. The book names these fruits: apples, bananas, mangoes and guavas, and these vegetables: carrots, potatoes, pumpkins, peas, cauliflowers and turnips. The season and colour for the student's own choices are not stated in the book.

Activity (book p. 59)

Q: Activity: Give the following information about your favourite game: i. What is your favourite game? ii. Why do you like this game? iii. Where do you play this game? iv. At which time do you play? v. How many players participate in it? vi. What are your feelings after you finish your game?

Ans: Note: This is a personal/oral activity about the student's own favourite game, so it has no fixed written answer in the book. The book only tells us that exercise is important for children, for example riding a bicycle, swimming, and playing different sports like football and volleyball, and that regular exercise keeps the body strong and healthy and protects it from diseases.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Plants prepare their own food in the presence of sunlight; this process is called photosynthesis.
  • Food which contains all the basic groups of food is called a balanced diet.
  • Milk is a complete diet and is necessary for strong teeth and bones.
  • For a healthy life, balanced diet, cleanliness, proper sleep and regular exercise are necessary.

Q1. Choose the correct option. (book p. 60)

Q: i. Different organisms eat _____ food. (a) same (b) different (c) balanced

Ans: different

Q: ii. Polar bear is _____ animal. (a) herbivore (b) omnivores (c) carnivores

Ans: carnivores

Q: iii. On the basis of food consumption animals are divided into _____ groups. (a) 3 (b) 4 (c) 5

Ans: 3

Q: iv. For good health taking bath _____ is necessary. (a) regularly (b) sometimes (c) every month

Ans: regularly

Q: v. Animals are called _____ which eat meat, plants and fruits. (a) omnivores (b) herbivores (c) carnivores

Ans: omnivores

Q2. Write T for true and F for false (book p. 60)

Q: True or False: i. Balanced diet is important for good health.

Ans: True

Q: True or False: ii. Fruits preservation method is not too old.

Ans: False

Q: True or False: iii. Different fresh fruits are available throughout the year.

Ans: False

Q: True or False: iv. Keeping home clean is only the duty of parents.

Ans: False

Q: True or False: v. For good health, balanced diet along with proper sleep is important.

Ans: True

Q3. Encircle the pictures (book p. 61)

Q: Q3. Encircle the pictures of carnivores with red, herbivores with green and omnivores with yellow colour.

Ans: Note: This is a colouring activity done on the pictures in the book, so it has no written answer. The book itself gives these examples to help: Herbivores eat grass, plants and their fruit — goat, cow, rabbit. Carnivores eat the meat of other animals — lion, cheetah, wolf. Omnivores eat meat, plants and their fruits — ostrich, rat, crow.

Q4. Answer the following questions. (book p. 62)

Q: i. Where do plants get their food from?

Ans: Plants prepare their own food in the presence of sunlight. This process is called photosynthesis. All other living organisms depend directly or indirectly on plants for their food.

Q: ii. What is balanced diet?

Ans: Food which contains all the basic groups of food is called a balanced diet. It contains fruits, vegetables, grains, meat, milk and eggs etc. We need such a diet for a healthy and active life.

Q: iii. Give four examples of fresh and dry fruits each.

Ans: Fresh fruits: apple, banana, mango and guava. Dry fruits: nuts, almonds, peanuts and pistachio. These are the examples given in the book.

Q: iv. Why is milk necessary for children?

Ans: Milk is a complete diet. It is necessary for strong teeth and bones. For growing babies, milk is the most important diet, so it is very necessary for children.

Q: v. What measures are necessary for healthy life?

Ans: For a healthy life, a balanced diet, cleanliness, proper sleep and regular exercise are necessary. We should wash our hands with soap, brush our teeth daily, wear neat and clean clothes, take a bath regularly, cut our nails, and keep our room, surroundings and plates of food clean.

Practical Work (book p. 62)

Q: Practical Work: Arrange cleanliness competition among children once a month. Give prizes to students getting 1st, 2nd and 3rd position in body cleanliness (nail, hair, clothes etc.), and cleanliness of things (bag, chair, table etc.).

Ans: Note: This is a practical class activity, so it has no written answer. It is done in the classroom once a month, as described in the book.

chapters.title: The Role of Government and Citizens

lessons.title: Government, Citizens and Good Citizens
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • We cannot do all the work ourselves; people work for each other in a society.
  • Government institutions named in the book are schools, hospitals, army, police, post offices and banks.
  • The government establishes these institutions for the welfare of the people.
  • A good citizen always speaks the truth, is honest, respects the law and takes care of the rights of others.
  • Good people make a good society.

Think and tell / Activity (book p. 64)

Q: Think and tell whether: Can we grow grain for ourselves? Can we build our homes ourselves? Can we sew our clothes ourselves? Can you treat yourself, if you are sick? Can we make our daily use items and instruments ourselves?

Ans: No, we cannot do all these things ourselves. Humans live together to meet their needs. They work for each other's welfare and development. For example, the teacher teaches children, the doctor treats patients and the farmer grows grains.

Q: Activity: Tell about five people in your neighbourhood, how they work for the local population (society)?

Ans: Note: This is an oral/personal activity about the student's own neighbourhood, so it has no single fixed written answer in the book. The book gives these examples of people working for society: a teacher teaches children, a doctor treats patients, and a farmer grows grains. People work in different ways for the development and improvement of their society.

Activity (book p. 66)

Q: Write names of few government institutions in your area and tell what they do for the people.

Ans: The book names these government institutions: schools, hospitals, army, police, post offices and banks. The government establishes these institutions for the welfare of the people, and these institutions serve people according to their needs. The government is responsible to provide basic needs to its people and work for their welfare.

Activity: Good Citizen (book p. 67)

Q: Activity: Good Citizen — paste your picture and think and tell, in addition to the qualities described in the book, what other qualities do you have?

Ans: Note: This is a personal/paste-picture and oral activity, so it has no fixed written answer in the book. The book describes a good citizen like this: a good citizen is one who works for the improvement of his country and its people. He loves them. He believes in equality, truth and respect for law. A good citizen always speaks the truth, is honest, takes care of the rights of others, respects the law, is responsible, takes care of the environment, forgives others, avoids quarrelling, fulfils his duties properly, is loyal to his country, believes in providing men and women the same opportunities for development, and respects his elders and teachers. Good people make a good society.

Think! (book p. 68)

Q: Think! Every person in the society is important. i. What if sweeper does not clean-up for a few days? ii. If there is no puncture mechanic, what problems will be created for us?

Ans: Note: The book does not give a direct written answer to these two questions. It only states that every person in the society is important, and that humans live together to meet their needs and work for each other's welfare and development. The student is asked to think and tell the answer in class.

Q2. Complete the chart (book p. 69)

Q: Q2. Complete the chart: Government Responsibilities (write four responsibilities).

Ans: Four responsibilities of the government, as given in the book, are: 1) To provide basic needs to its people. 2) To work for the welfare and development of the people. 3) To establish institutions such as schools, hospitals, army, police, post offices and banks. 4) To provide many facilities for the welfare of the people, so that these institutions serve people according to their needs.

Q4. Give short answers to the following questions. (book p. 69)

Q: i. Why educational institutions are established?

Ans: Educational institutions are established so that people can get education. Quality education is the fundamental right of every citizen. A society can make development only if its people are educated and healthy, so the government establishes schools for the welfare of the people.

Q: ii. Why government is necessary?

Ans: Government is necessary because it provides many facilities for the welfare and development of the people. People form government to get these things done. The government is responsible to provide basic needs to its people and work for their welfare.

Q: iii. How a good society is formed?

Ans: A good society is formed by good people. Humans live together to meet their needs and work for each other's welfare and development. Living together in such a way makes a society, and good people make a good society.

lessons.title: Understanding Disagreements
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • At home, siblings sometimes disagree on the use and ownership of things; at school, students may disagree on seats in the class.
  • Guidelines for resolving disagreements: keep calm, listen carefully, respect others, control your anger, admit and apologize for your mistakes, and forgive others.
  • Common reasons for disagreements are not listening carefully, no respect for the opinion of others and misunderstanding.
  • These are personal and practical activities based on the student's own experience.

Activity (book p. 73)

Q: Activity: Understand the differences among people in your home, school and neighbourhood and explain what types of differences generally occur. Fill the table: Disagreements at home, Disagreements at school, Disagreements in neighbourhood.

Ans: Note: This is a practical table-filling activity based on your own observation, so there is no single fixed answer. The book gives these examples: at home, siblings sometimes disagree on the use and ownership of things; at school, disagreement is found among students on seats in the class. The book does not give a fixed example for the neighbourhood.

Activity (book p. 74)

Q: Activity: Make different expression of face to show emotions such as happiness, grief, sadness, annoyance and hatred etc.

Ans: Note: This is a practical classroom activity with no written answer. Students make facial expressions to show emotions such as happiness, grief, sadness, annoyance and hatred.

Activity (book p. 75)

Q: Activity: What should be done in addition to the guidelines described above to resolve disagreements? (Guidelines in the book: resolve the disagreements properly, forgiving others for their mistakes, respect others, listen carefully to others, keep calm, talking on your own turn, control over anger, talk slowly, admit your mistakes, apologize for your mistakes.)

Ans: Note: This is an open activity. The book lists the guidelines shown in the question but does not state any additional points beyond them, so no further answer is given in the book.

Activity (book p. 77)

Q: Activity i. Keeping in view the disagreements with a friend during the game in playground: What was the disagreement?

Ans: Note: This is a personal activity based on your own experience in the playground. The book does not give one fixed disagreement; each student writes about his or her own disagreement.

Q: Activity ii. What was the main reason of disagreement?

Ans: Note: This depends on your own experience. The book lists common reasons for disagreements, such as not listening to others carefully, no respect for the opinion of others, misunderstanding, and differences in likes and dislikes. Write the reason that fits your own case.

Q: Activity iii. How the disagreement resolved?

Ans: Note: This depends on your own experience. The book says disagreements can be resolved by listening carefully to each other, thinking over it, keeping calm, talking on your own turn, and by the problem-solving method: stop and talk, listen, think, choose from options, and ask an elder if you are not satisfied.

Q: Activity iv. How did you feel when the disagreements resolved?

Ans: Note: This is a personal feeling and has no single fixed answer in the book. Each student writes how he or she felt when the disagreement was resolved.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • When people have different views on the same issue, it is called disagreement.
  • If disagreements are not resolved, they can grow into conflicts and can lead to a fight.
  • The problem-solving method is: stop and talk, listen, think, choose from options, and ask an elder if you are not satisfied.
  • When you are wrong, admit your mistake and apologize for it.

Q1. Think and describe. (book p. 78)

Q: i. What would you do if disagreement arises between your two friends?

Ans: I would help them resolve it in a good manner. I would ask them to keep calm, listen carefully to each other, respect each other's opinion and think over it. The book says disagreements can be resolved by discussion and by the problem-solving method.

Q: ii. What would you do if you come to know that you were wrong?

Ans: I would admit my mistake and apologize for my mistake. The book's guidelines for resolving disagreements say: admit your mistakes and apologize for your mistakes.

Q: iii. If disagreement arise between you and your friend and you fail to convince him, what would you do?

Ans: I would use the problem-solving method: calm down, talk and listen respectfully, and think in a positive way. If I am still not satisfied, the book says to ask an elder to solve the problem.

Q: iv. If you have disagreement with your friend and your friend is wrong, what would you do?

Ans: I would listen carefully to my friend, respect him, talk slowly and keep calm. I would also forgive my friend for his mistake, because the book's guidelines say to forgive others for their mistakes and to respect others.

Q: v. If two of your friends quarrel, whom would you support?

Ans: Note: The book does not state whom to support when two friends quarrel, so no fixed answer is given in the book. The book only teaches that disagreements should be resolved properly by listening carefully, keeping calm and controlling anger.

Q2. Keeping in mind your disagreements at home, school or somewhere else with others, mark in the relevant box. (book p. 78)

Q: Q2. When I have disagreement with someone else then: i. I am responsible for the disagreements. ii. I control my anger. iii. I try to blame others for the mistake. iv. Listen to others carefully. v. If I am wrong, I admit it. vi. If the mistake is of other, I forgive. vii. I hate the quarreler. viii. I try to resolve the disagreements in a good manner. (Mark Never / Rarely / Always for each.)

Ans: Note: This is a personal self-check activity with no single correct answer. Each student marks Never, Rarely or Always honestly for himself or herself. The book teaches the good habits in this list: control over anger, listening carefully to others, admitting your mistake, forgiving others, and resolving disagreements in a good manner.

Q3. Give short answer to the following questions. (book p. 79)

Q: i. What is meant by disagreement?

Ans: When people have different views on the same issue and do not agree on any one point, it is called disagreement. In other words, when the opinion of two or more people on a single matter is different, it is called disagreement.

Q: ii. Write down any three reasons for disagreements?

Ans: Three reasons for disagreements given in the book are: (1) not listening to others carefully, (2) no respect for the opinion of others, and (3) creation of misunderstanding. Other reasons in the book are not fulfilling one's duty properly, not waiting for one's turn, unrealization of desires, and differences in likes and dislikes.

Q: iii. Who settles the disagreements at your home?

Ans: Note: This depends on your own home, so the book gives no single name. The book's problem-solving method says that if you are not satisfied, you should ask an elder to solve the problem, so at home an elder settles the disagreement.

Q: iv. How can we settle disagreements?

Ans: We can settle disagreements by keeping calm, controlling our anger, listening carefully to others, respecting others, talking slowly and on our own turn, admitting and apologizing for our mistakes, and forgiving others for their mistakes. We can also resolve them through discussion and the problem-solving method.

Q: v. What is the result if disagreements are not resolved?

Ans: If disagreements are not resolved, they can grow into conflicts and can lead to a fight. The book says disagreements can lead to fight if not resolved, and if conflicts are not resolved, they turn into fight.

lessons.title: States of Matter
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A solid has a specific shape and a specific volume, for example a stone.
  • A liquid has no specific shape and takes the shape of its container, but it has a specific volume, for example water.
  • A gas has no specific shape and no specific volume, for example air.
  • On heating, ice changes into water, and on heating more, water changes into water vapours.
  • Change in the state of matter occurs due to change in temperature.

Think! (book p. 80)

Q: Think! Take a few ice cubes and put them in a jug of water. The ice cubes will start swimming in water, why?

Ans: Note: The book asks this as a thinking question but does not state the reason in its text, so no answer is given in the book.

Activity (book p. 82)

Q: Activity: Select one thing from each state of matter in your surrounding. Observe their different characteristics and write the results in the table (Matter / Shape / Volume for Solid, Liquid and Gas).

Ans: From the book's table of characteristics: Solid has a specific shape and a specific volume. Liquid has no specific shape and adopts the shape of the container in which it is placed, and it has a specific volume. Gas has no specific shape and adopts the shape of the container in which it is placed, and it has no specific volume. Examples from the book are stone (solid), water (liquid) and air (gas).

Practical Work (book p. 83)

Q: i. In the presence of your teacher, take some cubes of ice in beaker and heat it. To which state does the ice change?

Ans: On heating, the ice changes from the solid state into the liquid state, that is, ice changes into water.

Q: ii. Heat it more and observe the changes which occurs?

Ans: On heating more, the water changes into water vapours, that is, into the gaseous state.

Q: iii. Why did the changes in ice occur?

Ans: The changes in ice occurred due to the change in temperature. The book says change in matter occurs due to the change in temperature, and the state of matter can be changed due to temperature.

mcqs.q: A solid has _____.
options: a specific shape and a specific volume
mcqs.why: From the book's table of characteristics: a solid has a specific shape and a specific volume. Stone is an example of a solid.

options: a specific shape and a specific volume
no specific shape but a specific volume
mcqs.why: A liquid has no specific shape and adopts the shape of the container in which it is placed, and it has a specific volume. Water is an example of a liquid.

mcqs.q: A gas has _____.
options: no specific shape and no specific volume
a specific shape and a specific volume
mcqs.why: A gas has no specific shape and adopts the shape of the container in which it is placed, and it has no specific volume. Air is an example of a gas.

mcqs.why: In the practical work, ice cubes are heated in a beaker in the presence of the teacher. On heating, the ice changes from the solid state into the liquid state, that is, ice changes into water.

mcqs.q: On heating more, water changes into _____.
mcqs.why: On heating more, the water changes into water vapours, that is, into the gaseous state.

mcqs.why: The changes in ice occurred due to the change in temperature. The book says change in matter occurs due to the change in temperature.

mcqs.why: Examples from the book are stone (solid), water (liquid) and air (gas). Milk is also a liquid.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a gas?
mcqs.why: Air is a gas. It has no specific shape and no specific volume. Stone and wood are solids and water is a liquid.

options: the container in which it is placed
mcqs.why: A liquid has no specific shape and adopts the shape of the container in which it is placed, and it has a specific volume.

mcqs.why: The book says the state of matter can be changed due to temperature, for example ice (solid) changes into water (liquid) and then into vapours (gas) on heating.

lessons.title: End of Chapter Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Anything which occupies space and has mass is called matter.
  • Water exists in the liquid state and vapours are the gas state of matter.
  • Milk, honey, juice and tea are liquids; pencil, apple, football and chair are solids.
  • The gaseous state is used during breathing, because we breathe in air.
  • A lighted candle melts because of the heat of the flame; the melted wax becomes solid again on cooling.

Q1. Fill in the blanks. (book p. 84)

Q: i. Water exists in the _____ state of matter.

Ans: liquid

Q: ii. Solid contains _____ shape.

Ans: specific

Q: iii. All matters have _____.

Ans: mass

Q: iv. Due to _____ in temperature, the ice changes into water.

Ans: increase

Q: v. Due to increase in temperature the state of _____ changes.

Ans: matter

Q2. In the given pictures differentiate solid, liquid and gas also write the state of matter below each picture. (book pp. 84-85)

Q: Picture 1 (book p. 84): Balloon. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Gas. The air filled in the balloon is a gas.

Q: Picture 2 (book p. 84): Juice being poured into a glass. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Liquid. Juice is a liquid.

Q: Picture 3 (book p. 84): Black chair. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Solid. A chair is a solid.

Q: Picture 4 (book p. 84): Wooden chair. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Solid. A chair is a solid.

Q: Picture 5 (book p. 84): Smoke rising from factory chimneys. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Gas. Smoke is in the gaseous state.

Q: Picture 6 (book p. 84): Honey in a jar with a spoon. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Liquid. Honey is a liquid.

Q: Picture 7 (book p. 85): Milk/liquid being poured into a cup. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Liquid.

Q: Picture 8 (book p. 85): Car. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Solid. A car is a solid.

Q: Picture 9 (book p. 85): Smoke/cloud in the sky. Write the state of matter.

Ans: Gas. Smoke and vapours are in the gaseous state.

Q: i. Vapours are the _____ state of matter. (a) solid (b) liquid (c) gas

Ans: gas

Q: ii. Anything which occupies space and having _____ is called matter. (a) mass (b) specific shape (c) colour

Ans: mass

Q: iii. Water is the _____ state of matter. (a) gas (b) solid (c) liquid

Ans: liquid

Q: iv. The thing which has specific shape and volume is called _____. (a) solid (b) liquid (c) gas

Ans: solid

Ans: Liquid

Q: Pencil — State of matter?

Ans: Solid

Q: Water vapours — State of matter?

Ans: Gas

Q: Air in the balloon — State of matter?

Ans: Gas

Q: Apple — State of matter?

Ans: Solid

Q: Honey — State of matter?

Ans: Liquid

Q: Football — State of matter?

Ans: Solid

Q: Tea — State of matter?

Ans: Liquid

Q5. Write short answers. (book p. 86)

Q: i. Explain the characteristics of solid.

Ans: A solid has a specific shape and a specific volume.

Q: ii. How matter can be changed from one state to another?

Ans: Matter can be changed from one state to another by changing the temperature. The book says the state of matter can be changed due to temperature, for example ice (solid) changes into water (liquid) and then into vapours (gas) on heating.

Q: iii. Explain the shape of gas.

Ans: Gas has no specific shape. It adopts the shape of the container in which it is placed. Gas also has no specific volume.

Q: iv. What is the main difference between solid and liquid?

Ans: The main difference is of shape. A solid has a specific shape, while a liquid has no specific shape and adopts the shape of the container in which it is placed. Both solid and liquid have a specific volume.

Q: v. Which state of matter is used during breathing?

Ans: The gaseous state is used during breathing, because we breathe in air, and air is a gas. The book gives air as an example of matter.

Practical Work (book p. 87)

Q: i. Take a candle. Candle is solid because it has a definite shape and volume. Now light the candle. What changes occur in the candle?

Ans: On lighting, the candle melts. Its solid wax starts changing into liquid wax.

Q: ii. Why this change occurs in it?

Ans: This change occurs due to the heat of the flame, that is, due to the increase in temperature. The book says the state of matter can be changed due to temperature.

Q: iii. After some time the melting candle changes into which state of matter?

Ans: After some time, the melted liquid wax cools down and changes back into the solid state.

Q: iv. Why this change occurs?

Ans: This change occurs due to the decrease in temperature when the melted wax cools. The book says change in matter occurs due to the change in temperature.

mcqs.why: The gaseous state is used during breathing, because we breathe in air, and air is a gas. The book gives air as an example of matter.

lessons.title: Sources of Energy and Their Uses
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • No work can be done without the use of energy.
  • The Sun is the biggest source of energy; its energy is used for the production of electricity.
  • Coal is used for heating, light, cooking food, running trains and ships, and producing electricity.
  • Energy from flowing water is used in water mills and in dams such as Tarbela, Warsak and Mangla to produce electricity.
  • Natural gas is used to keep houses warm, cook food, and run factories and vehicles.
  • Most sources of energy are limited, so electricity, gas and water shall be used according to the needs.

Think! (book p. 91)

Q: Think! If there were no sources of energy (coal, natural gas, water) how the world would have been?

Ans: The book says no work can be done without the use of energy, and energy is required for tools to work. So without sources of energy, no work could be done and our tools and machines could not work.

Activity (book p. 91)

Q: Activity: Write the uses of the source: Sun.

Ans: The Sun is the biggest source of energy. Its energy reaches the Earth through rays in the form of heat and light. This solar energy is used for the production of electricity.

Q: Activity: Write the uses of the source: Coal.

Ans: Coal has been used for centuries for heating, light and cooking food. Coal is used for running trains and ships, and now coal is used for the production of electricity.

Q: Activity: Write the uses of the source: Water.

Ans: Energy is present in flowing water. It is used for grinding grains in a water mill. Nowadays, dams are built on rivers to produce electricity, for example Tarbela, Warsak and Mangla dams in Pakistan.

Q: Activity: Write the uses of the source: Natural gas.

Ans: Natural gas is used to keep houses warm, cook food, run factories and vehicles.

Activity (book p. 94)

Q: Activity: Teacher shall divide the class into four groups, name the first group water, second as gas, third one as electricity and the fourth as oil. Each group shall tell how it helps human beings and which precautions shall be kept in mind while using it.

Ans: Note: This is an oral group activity with no single written answer. The book's 'Keep in Mind' note states the factual point for precautions: most sources of energy such as coal, gas, oil and water are limited, therefore use electricity, gas and water according to the needs.

lessons.title: Life in the Stone Age
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • People of the stone age ate uncooked meat because they did not know how to make fire and cook food.
  • Their food was plants, fruits and uncooked meat.
  • The invention of the wheel and the discovery of metals paved the way for human development.
  • Visiting a museum and pasting pictures are practical activities.

Q: Why people of stone age ate uncooked meat?

Ans: People of the stone age ate uncooked meat because they did not know how to make fire and cook food. The book says that with the passage of time man learned making of fire and cooking food. Their food was plants, fruits and uncooked meat.

Ans: Note: This is a practical visit and essay-writing activity, so it has no fixed written answer in the book. The book only says that the life style, dress, food, source of transportation and methods of communication of people of old age were completely different from the present age.

Ans: Note: The book does not give a direct answer to this question. It only says that the invention of wheel and discovery of metals paved the way for human development, and that present life is very comfortable and safe than the past because of continuous human struggle.

lessons.title: Inventions Around Us
